item.title: Four hidden dimensions of effective teams
item.description: Company success isn’t about following a magic formula or hacking the corporate game; it’s about using the context and information around us with purpose.Building this simple new tool helped me validate a long-standing personal belief: stop accepting that designers only generate value through “cosmetics.”This year, I had the honor of joining a revolutionary LATAM design convention in Lima, Perú, where I was invited to speak about design and team strategy, two topics I’m most passionate about.Months before the convention, I reflected on how to send a strong message that sparks questions and encourages the audience to take action to increase design’s influence in corporate decision-making, something we (the designers) have long believed we deserve by right.One topic I highlighted during the talk was an artifact I developed early this year that helped me bridge design and company strategy and brought me closer to strategic conversations, with promising results so far.Building this simple new tool helped me validate a long-standing personal belief: stop accepting that designers only generate value through “cosmetics,” since some people still think design is just the visual layer of functionality.The common language in all companies.One idea that resonated strongly with the audience was the fact that everything we do as designers has a monetary consequence (it shouldn’t be a novelty nowadays), no matter the size of the solution, idea, or context; so thinking in numbers is one thing that should be embraced from junior design positions. Numbers aren’t just money from users; they’re everything that produces it. In that sense, developing the self-awareness to understand and measure our own work towards results could put us in a strategic position within a company.How to measure effectiveness? The four dimensions you overlook.This isn’t just about having KPIs or OKRs in a team; it’s about understanding all measurable resources that show how effective we are as a company.I’ve identified some basic dimensions that define an entire company’s dynamics and, with them, all the possible challenges within. Although these dimensions seem obvious in every company, after 20+ years in the tech industry, the truth is they aren’t, and we still struggle, over and over, with the same old issues.How did this perspective come about? Well, it wasn’t really a discovery, but rather connecting disparate dots—things people overlooked when executing projects or having conversations.I ask my teammates a few basic questions that can paint a picture of a company or team’s state. I used to ask these questions informally, but I didn’t always have a complete picture of the overall situation. That is why, after some time, I decided to organize a set of measurable dimensions that could clearly diagnose my environment and its main challenges.The sum of all dimensions is a metric that reflects the maturity and effectiveness level of a company or its teams, helping build a solid foundation for product creation and making the process more rewarding.Use this metric to acknowledge the state of the company and start having relevant conversations:The StructureIt delimits the field of action and its actors.The first dimension refers to how people, teams, or areas are connected; it comes first because it reveals the system we are working in, including both positive and negative factors.The structure dimension is built from inner concepts that, together, give us a full picture of how the system of connection works. Why is this dimension important? Because it delimits the field of action and its actors.1. Role definitionThis is the first aspect I ask when I want to understand the state of a team; it is surprisingly common to encounter companies and teams that lack information regarding this fundamental concept. For some reason, some people consider it normal to hire someone with no plan for the company or the professional.The lack of information about a role reveals the company’s level of corporate maturity. At this point, we can find several reasons regarding this issue: “We are in a digital transformation, so we’re figuring out the design roles,” “We brought you here (the leader) to help us build the team vision,” “This team originally was under the CMO or CTO management, and his/her knowledge was limited in terms of user experience,” “We are a startup, we wear a lot of hats, so you build your own role.”Some of those reasons may be valid, but my critique around this is a simple question: how do you move for years (sometimes under a lot of stress) without knowing your boundaries or responsibilities? I’ve seen a lot of designers immersed in constant uncertainty because they don’t know their range of actions, all disguised under the condescending phrase: “I do what I’m asked.”I think not having a role makes you vulnerable to whatever circumstances arise, which, in my opinion, is highly detrimental to professional growth because your job keeps changing.A clear understanding of product roles lays the foundation for how effective teams operate within a system.2. Career pathMoving forward, the career path is the next level of structure maturity in teams or companies. Part of my assessment when joining a team is understanding all possible growth tracks within the Structure I’ll lead. When a career path is missing, the negative effects might be several.In the short term, the impact might not be as visible, so people could feel “comfortable” for a couple of years, but the thing with this issue is that time is inevitable; eventually, when years have passed, people will realize they are way behind the latest skills in the market, which will create great frustration and a sense of wasting valuable time doing the same job without increasing their talents.3. Org chartKnowing who to report to, who to lead, or who to work with as a peer matters. Part of being effective is knowing who to talk to to drive results. Org charts are often dead, outdated documentation; people only see them the first week of a new job. Over time, I’ve realized this artifact is fundamental for decision-making or showing results. From a design perspective, org charts can also be stakeholder maps or the canvas for making strategic decisions for the team.If org charts aren’t visible in a production dynamic, effective communication is almost impossible, and the consequences will hit sooner or later. That said, here’s the latest concept for the structure dimension.4. Working flowsImagine you have a clear understanding of your team’s structure, but communication isn’t always effective. Why? Well, it is because we haven’t connected the roles into a functional dynamic, and without that, we have nothing; imagine a classical orchestra without a director; it’s quite a mess.Designers are experts at figuring out user flows to connect a product with clients, but they don’t think to do the same exercise to connect roles on a team to other teams towards a product goal. Strong working flows make product decisions more effective, and time will be your ally.PerformanceIt is obvious we need to talk about performance as the second effective dimension, but far from having KPIs, this approach is different; it is about how much we know about success for the company and us. As for the structure, the performance dimension has inner concepts that feed into the overall dimension, and I’ll guide you through each one.1. Company goalI’ve been part of projects where this information is nonexistent, or teams aren’t aware of it and make decisions with a biased vision; the result? Narrowed approaches, sometimes disconnected from the main company strategic plan; sooner or later, the consequences of working away from what the company is pursuing can be expensive.We used to think the company’s goal was something shared in an all-hands meeting, and then nobody remembered it. Still, keeping this goal present in every project helps us filter hard decisions and create more accurate, business-driven developments. Bring these goals to the next project pitch, and stakeholders will embrace your idea more than if you pitch something amazing but far from a business priority.2. Area and team goalsDigging deep into goals, the next level is the area goals. This information is more visible than company goals. They are closer to us since we operate in a more tactical field, but remember that area goals should build toward the company objective, so being aware of the previous concept matters.Are you aware of this information when executing something? I would say most teammates will say, “I’m not sure,” so don’t assume they are clueless about this.Why do I bother to highlight this concept? The answer lies in how other members of the company still perceive our work: as something merely aesthetic, rather than an effort toward effectiveness and conversion. I’d wager that if designers approached a board of directors with a strategy focused on business objectives, the results would be different.3. Installed capacityI’ve said it before, and I’ll keep pointing out this issue: are we reactive, or do we have the capacity to react? Hard pill to swallow, right? It is sad to see how design leaders just follow in a huge reactive storm, where the day-to-day is about surviving others’ mess.Not knowing your team’s capacity or your teammates’ capacity compels you to follow orders without negotiation, which is, most of the time, negative in every way.As a leader, discussing capacity reveals more about you than you think; it gives you power and control over the project’s time and decisions. On the contrary, not knowing this information, as I said before, makes you accept others’ conditions with no chance to state your point of view.4. Definition of success/failureHow do you know your team is doing right? Or wrong? Are you one of those who go with the flow? Some days we’re good, and some days everything stinks. This concept has nothing to do with accomplishing OKRs; it’s about having clear team boundaries: what to celebrate and what to penalize.This concept should be repeatedly visible on every team, and it should become the DNA for how we operate and behave in front of others.Building a healthy DNA for the team will create a reputation for you and your team, something that can be well rewarded in company strategic moments.TimeThe third dimension is about knowing the time we expend doing something. As you may know, time is money, and not being aware of it can lead us to an ineffective spiral with negative consequences.One way to figure out how ineffective teams are in terms of time is simple: in ongoing projects, there is often no awareness of stages or changes that come in at the wrong time and slow down the team’s output. In these scenarios, a medium initiative can become large, expensive, and frustrating for teams.The concepts that build the time dimensions are related to hours and their usage:1. Team execution hoursThis concept is about tracking how much time the team spends on projects; this information is usually overlooked in strategic conversations, and without it, we can’t measure how fast the team is or how long projects take.Tracking team effort over time will give us a better perspective on how to respond to future challenges, so that the next time we face a project, we’ll be ready to provide a better time estimate.In planning sessions with the team, having a project time matrix will give the team a solid starting point instead of jumping into the unknown without a clue how long this challenge will last.2. Strategy hoursThe other side of time is what we spend on conversations, planning, or solving situations for the team. In senior design positions, this time is crucial to account for; we will not always be able to execute tasks if our job demands that we oversee multiple teams or duties.I recommend having some sort of artifact that can back you up when showing results to execs; whether execution or strategic time, it is important to be aware of the amount of time (money) you represent for the company.MoneySince time is money, other monetary situations shouldn’t be strange for us. Not knowing anything about money (the common language in companies) will relegate us to a merely executing position. At the same time, other profiles will discuss whether it is profitable to take on a project.We don’t need to be financial experts to understand our resource costs, and that’s enough. Some of the basic notions of money issues to control are:1. Team and role costHow much does your team cost? It is a question that is not always on our radar. Still, once you realize you have a team cost of X, you can approach project planning from a different perspective, especially when comparing it with budgets.If you apply this information to your planning conversations, you can make smarter moves in hiring people or shifting resources across multiple initiatives.2. Projects budgetIn some decision tables, every conversation, context, or challenge starts with the budget, so you should understand the project’s financial scope from the beginning.This information may not be attractive to junior design positions, but for leaders, it is crucial to manage and understand.Money and time are rare areas of knowledge among designers, so developing them will put us on a different level when approaching projects or hard conversations in companies.My takeaway from this:There are several aptitudes we can adopt to thrive in companies, whether big or small; the goal is still the same: converting money. Around success in companies, there is way too much information from modern history to read and watch. Still, in design environments, which I think is fascinating, I feel like there is little information on how to use our expertise to our advantage in a strategic way; maybe I’m wrong, but if we’re still struggling to show our value in companies, it’s because we haven’t figured out how to back up our discipline, right?I believe the basics always work best, and the four dimensions of effective teams come from watching teams over 20 years of experience in different contexts and industries. Maybe this is not the holy formula for success, but at least it gives us a different perspective on how to use the information that is always there, but we don’t see or use, and let other people make decisions for us.To write this article, I want to credit all the fantastic information sources and other authors who have written about related topics, each from an exciting, different perspective.The 3 Cs of Coaching: The Foundation of Effective Team LeadershipBuilding Effective Teams Is Not About Hiring Based on Skills Only6 Essential Tips for Effective Team Collaboration — Win as one team!Four hidden dimensions of effective teams was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Who draws the in-betweens?
item.description: Every line we draw around AI measures the tool. Authorship has always lived in the decisions.Earlier this month Dior released Christian Dior’s Night in Color, a holiday short directed by Sylvain Chomet, the animator behind The Triplets of Belleville and The Illusionist. A week after release, the internet had already reached its verdict. People had paused, zoomed in, counted the fingers, and decided it was AI.https://medium.com/media/b0e597b691aae940498b481aa00feecb/hrefChomet and his producer, Aton Soumache, answered in an interview with Variety. Artists drew the characters, they say, the backgrounds and the key poses, and around twenty people worked on the film for seven months. Then came the detail that set everyone off. The team had used automated interpolation, software that generates the frames between keyframes, for what Soumache called “a very small part of the process.” Chomet said it automated the repetitive, mechanical side of animation and left the creative side alone.A lot of people read that as a confession, but for me it was something else. Until then, I’d mostly thought about AI the way people in my job usually do: as a question of tools, speed and budgets. This was the first time I looked at it through an artist’s eyes. I tried to imagine Chomet reading the accusations, a man who has spent his whole career drawing by hand, being told his film wasn’t his. And I think I understood what must have gone through his head in that moment: what is the difference?The Triplets of Belleville (2003), dir. Sylvain Chomet. Go ahead, count the fingers.His films have always had in-betweeners. Other people always drew part of his films, following his keys, his timing, his idea of how things should move. So if he drew the keys and a machine filled in some of the frames between them, is the film still his? And if it isn’t, where exactly did it stop being his?I want to try answering that honestly, by following the lines people usually draw and seeing whether they hold.The first line: a human hand on every frameThe instinctive answer is that art means a person drew it. But that has never been true of animation, which is why the Dior case is so useful.For most of its history, hand-drawn animation has worked like this: A lead animator draws the key poses, the drawings that carry the action and the acting. Assistants and in-betweeners fill in the frames between them, sometimes dozens for every second of film. Their names sit far down the credits, when they appear at all, and I’ve never heard anyone leave a cinema praising an in-between. The lead animator’s job is to direct. They decide how every movement should feel, look at every pass, push back on whatever doesn’t work, and keep going until the whole film looks like it came from a single hand.The lead animator draws the keys. Everything between them is someone else’s job. (Illustration by the author, made with the help of AI)So the “human hand on every frame” line was already crossed decades ago, by other humans nobody credited. Swapping some of those humans for software leaves the lead animator doing exactly the same job. The keys are still theirs and so is every decision about what stays and what gets redrawn. What changes is speed and cost, and I don’t see how speed makes a drawing less yours. Anyone who animated in Flash in the 2000s used tweens, automated in-betweening under another name, and nobody called it the end of the craft.To be fair to the critics, some frames really were ugly, and some of the flaws looked a lot like what people have learned to recognize as AI artifacts. Maybe the interpolation produced them, maybe not. But these things on their own prove very little. Chomet explained that extra fingers appear when you’re selling fast movement, and any animator will tell you the same. Smears and multiples are an old trick. If counting fingers were the test, half of classic cartoons from the 1930s would be guilty.Smears and multiples: frames that were never meant to be paused, only felt in motion. (Bosko in Person, Warner Bros., 1933. Via Bloop Animation)Hand-drawn in-betweens have always had their bad frames too. Pause almost any classic cartoon and you’ll find a face that collapses for a frame or a hand that melts into the next pose. Somebody drew those, worked against a deadline, and nobody checked closely enough. We forgive them because we watch the film, not individual frames. Imperfections in a production people love read as charm, or as the cost of making something. The same imperfections in a production people already suspect read as evidence.The second line: the machine has to be under controlThe more elaborate version of the objection goes like this: Fine, tools have always done part of the work, but those tools were predictable. A generative model isn’t, so using it means accepting whatever comes out.Animation has a good test case for this: hair and fur. Ever since Sulley’s coat in Monsters, Inc., a whole genre of films has existed partly to show off how good fur simulation had become. Nobody draws those hairs: artists define the groom, density, length and how it moves, and a simulation computes millions of strands frame by frame. The result is about as machine-made as an image gets, but we call it craft, because the artist decided what the fur should be and the software carried it out.From bare model to fur: the artist styles a few guide curves, maps the points, Houdini generates the rest. (Images: SideFX, Houdini documentation)I don’t think generative tools are as far from that as people assume. When I describe a shot to one of the video tools I use, say a rooftop at dusk with a slow push-in on a woman looking at the city, I don’t get a random picture, I get something close to what I described, similar to the way a camera operator brings back something close to your brief. Then the real work starts, because these tools now sit inside an ordinary editor. I can retime the push-in, cut the shot shorter, regrade the sky, rework the sound, and each of those changes does exactly what I tell it to.Photographers have lived with this forever: on the street you don’t control the light, the passers-by or the clouds, but you choose the moment, the frame and the edit. Nobody says the photo isn’t yours because you didn’t place the pedestrians. Nobody controls everything, not photographers, not animators, not anyone. What matters is whether you shaped the result, and AI doesn’t change that.In this beautiful photograph by Hannah Cauhepe on Unsplash, the train, the light and the blur all happened on their own. Where to stand, when to shoot and how long to keep the shutter open were her choices.The third line: real work takes effortThis is the one I feel most personally, because it’s usually framed as being “on the side” of people like me.Some of the websites I design are the projects I live for, complex and animated and thought through down to the scroll, and those take weeks because the effort is the point. But creative work has always been tied to commissions and invoices, and next to those projects there’s a steady stream of small sites for businesses that can’t spend much or wait long. Anyone in my industry will tell you that most of the website market runs on templates. Someone buys a theme, changes the colors, fonts, copy and photos, and ships it. Nobody calls that a betrayal of craft. It’s a service sized to a budget.Webflow claims 7000+ between free and premium templates. (Screenshot: Webflow Marketplace)The same goes for the pieces inside a site. A signup flow or a checkout is a solved problem, built on patterns users expect to behave the same everywhere, and a “creative” checkout is usually a worse one. I’ve never built one from scratch for its own sake, I use a proven component, one made and shared precisely so people like me don’t have to reinvent it, and configure it to fit. If I generate that same standard pattern instead of cloning it, I genuinely can’t see what I’ve stolen, or from whom.Templates aren’t only a way to do less, either. Used well, they’re a floor. If the checkout, the navigation and the basic layout are already solved, the hours I’d have spent rebuilding them go into the parts nobody has seen before: the interaction that takes three days to tune, the animation that makes a site feel like the brand it belongs to. Generated components work the same way. Starting from something solid leaves more time and energy for going past it.Probably the checkout you’ve used most often. Nobody wants it to be creative. (Screenshot: Shopify checkout)We’ve also watched this happen before. When Webflow, Squarespace and WordPress spread, designers said they would kill the profession and make every site look alike. They were partly right about the second part: the cheap end of the market filled up with lookalikes. But something else happened that nobody predicted: a whole generation of designers came in through those tools. People who never learned to code, who would never have been hired by an agency, started building sites on their own, and some of them turned out to be very good. No-code didn’t lower the ceiling. It raised it, because more people with taste could finally reach it.Some work needs artistic value and effort, some just needs to exist and work. The same tools served both, and insisting on effort everywhere mostly makes the small client pay for our self-image.The fourth line: you need the skillIf effort isn’t the line, maybe skill is. You should at least be able to make the thing yourself.Ira Glass has a well-known idea about this, often called “the taste gap”. People get into creative work because they have good taste, and for years their work falls short of it. The only way across that gap, he says, is to keep making work until your hands catch up. What I think generative tools do is close the gap from the other side. Say I can’t draw well, but I can sketch the character I want for my game. A tool helps me turn that sketch into a finished design, but it doesn’t get there on its own. I push it, version after version, deciding on the shoes, the hair, the eyes, the marks of its skin, until it looks exactly the way I imagined. The tool lent me its hands, but every decision was mine.Ira Glass said the only way through the gap is to do a lot of work. That part hasn’t changed, but how much work you can do has. (Illustration by the author, made with the help of AI)That deciding is the part that matters. As Nielsen Norman Group points out, these tools fill skill gaps, but being able to make something you couldn’t make before doesn’t mean it’s good.I live a version of this every week: I’d love to promote my work on social media with proper videos, with long cuts, animations timed to what I’m saying, captions that land on the right word, a title card that’s actually mine. I know what good looks like, because I watch plenty of it. What I don’t have is the budget to hire an editor for every post, and the honest alternative to a generated starting point was never a commissioned video, but rather no video at all.So I start from what the tools give me and work on it. Along the way I’m learning things I never had a reason to learn: what makes an intro hold people past the first seconds, how different montage styles change the pace, where a cut should fall so the point lands. Some editors will get less work because people like me can do this now, and I don’t pretend otherwise. But this particular job was never going to exist, because the money for it was never there. If anything, a self-made video that works is the kind of thing that eventually justifies hiring a professional for the bigger one.The worry is that skipping the struggle stunts people, the way pocket calculators were supposed to ruin arithmetic. They didn’t. Kids still learn math, and the ones who love it still go deep. Glass’s advice to make a lot of work still holds; you just get more rounds of making, judging and fixing in a year. The constraints don’t vanish, they move up, from “can I draw this hand” to “do I have anything worth saying.”Cheap making also means cheap failure, and that matters more than it sounds. If one of my videos flops, I’ve lost an afternoon, not a client budget, so I can afford to try the odd idea and see what happens. The same logic works at the top of the industry. Hollywood keeps making remakes because a film that costs two hundred million dollars has to be a safe bet. Lower the cost of making things and you lower the cost of taking a risk, which is usually where the original ideas come from.The fifth line: it learned from other people’s workThe last line people draw is about where the tools came from. Models were trained on artists’ work without asking, and for a lot of people that settles it.I’m aware this is an unpopular thing to say, but here’s my confession, if it is one: so was I. So was every artist who ever lived. Nothing we make comes from nowhere: it comes from everything I’ve seen, played, watched, read and lived through, other people’s work included, and nobody signed a release before any of it got into my head. The more varied that mix, the better the work tends to be. There’s even a name for it: the Medici Effect, from a 2004 book by Frans Johansson. It’s named after the Florentine banking family who, in the fifteenth century, funded sculptors, painters, architects, scientists, poets and philosophers and brought them together in the same city. Johansson’s argument is that the Renaissance came from that mixing, from ideas crossing between fields, more than from any single genius. Creativity mostly happens where influences meet.Ghibli is a good example for this. Isao Takahata and Hayao Miyazaki both said a French animated film, Paul Grimault’s La Bergère et le Ramoneur, later reworked as Le Roi et l’Oiseau, shaped how they thought about animation. Miyazaki once said that watching it taught him how to use space vertically. Grimault never gave permission, and nobody would call Castle in the Sky a Grimault film. The influence went in, got mixed with everything else they loved, and came out as something that was theirs.Influenced by someone else, but still unmistakably his own. (Castle in the Sky, Studio Ghibli, dir. Hayao Miyazaki, 1986)In March 2025 a new image model made “Ghibli style” the internet’s favorite filter, and for a few weeks it seemed everyone had turned their selfies, pets and memes into Miyazaki frames. Alongside them, an old clip came back: Miyazaki in 2016, watching a demo of AI-generated animation and calling it an insult to life itself. I respect that. He’s entitled to never want the technology anywhere near his work. But look at what the trend actually produced: millions of images that look like Ghibli, and not one of them is a Ghibli movie.That’s the part I think people miss. Even if I could draw perfect Ghibli-style cartoons, that wouldn’t make me Ghibli, or an artist. Ghibli is Ghibli because of its stories, its characters, its worlds, and a style that bends from film to film to serve them. A model can absorb the style, but that was never what made those films great.Millions of images can look like Ghibli. Not one of them is a Ghibli movie. (AI-generated with ChatGPT, uploaded by Anya2025 to Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0)There is one real difference, and I don’t want to skip it. When I learn from Miyazaki, I become one more artist with some of his influence in me. A model learns from everyone at once and can produce that influence on demand, for anyone, at almost no cost. That changes the market for people who draw for a living, and it’s a fair thing to worry about. Lost dog — or lost designer? on UX Collective presses on the same point, asking where influence ends, authorship begins and appropriation becomes exploitation, and it’s right that human learning and AI training aren’t the same thing. But that difference is an argument about markets, not authorship. The question this essay is asking is who made the thing, and a style on its own has never answered it.Where authorship actually livesPut those lines side by side and they share something. Every one of them measures the tool: whose hand, how predictable, how much effort, how much skill, what it learned from. Authorship has always been somewhere else, in the decisions.Designers have been circling this question since the first image generators. As Wait, who made this? notes, the questions about authorship, copyright and compensation raised by DALL-E and Midjourney still don’t have answers. Here’s the way of thinking about it that has helped me most.Think of any piece of work as a grid of small decisions: the shape, the color, the timing, the cut. Some cells you fill in yourself. The rest get filled by whatever you’re working with. A template fills them with someone else’s design choices, an in-betweener with their own hand, a fur simulator with physics, a model with patterns from its training data. Nobody fills in every cell, and nobody ever has.So instead of a line, I think there’s a matrix: the more of the grid you actually filled in yourself, the more of the work is yours. That explains why lazy AI art feels so empty, since almost none of its cells were decided by anyone. It also explains why Chomet’s film is Chomet’s, why my sketched character is mine, and why a template with the stock photos left in doesn’t really belong to anybody.From a one-line prompt to Chomet’s film: how much of each was actually decided. (Illustration by the author, made with the help of AI)It also explains what the backlash keeps getting wrong. From the outside nobody can see the decisions. A viewer can’t tell a character refined over days from one typed in a single line, so “contains AI” becomes shorthand for “nobody cared,” and the finger-counting starts. Sometimes the shorthand is right. Often, as with Dior, it lands on people who drew most of the film by hand.Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is an even clearer case. It was one of the most celebrated games of 2025, a debut from a studio that obviously poured itself into every frame, and it won Game of the Year at The Game Awards. Then it came out that the developer had used generative AI for a handful of placeholder textures, a few of which shipped by mistake and were patched out within days. The Indie Game Awards took back its Game of the Year and Debut Game prizes anyway. You can argue about the rules, but nobody who played that game could say nobody cared. And I don’t accept the framing that what we value is “knowing a human made it,” as if a machine in the pipeline erased the person. Every film of the last thirty years has had machines in the pipeline.Surely nobody can claim this game lacks authorship or intent. I don’t even like it, and I can see that. (Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, Sandfall Interactive, 2025)That puts some responsibility on us as creators. If people can’t see the process, we should show it. Dior’s campaign leaned on “traditional craftsmanship,” and Chomet said in Dior’s own promotional video that they work just like in the 1940s. Then an interview revealed software in the pipeline, and a good part of the anger came from finding out afterwards. Being open about how something was made costs nothing, and it’s the only way “they used AI” turns into a description instead of an accusation.What this means for people like meI’m not writing this from a safe distance. The small sites I build for clients on a budget are precisely the work these tools are learning to do, and I’d be lying if I said that doesn’t worry me. Some of that work will go away, and some of it is probably mine.It’s sad. It’s also true, and the first doesn’t change the second. There’s no version of this where the tools get un-invented and the market goes back to how it was. Portrait painters, typesetters and the ink-and-paint artists who colored animation cels by hand all went through some version of this, and none of them got the old world back by refusing to look at the new one. There will be more sameness too: research on AI-assisted writing found it helps weaker writers most while making their stories more alike. Designers are already seeing the interface version of this. AI made everyone a creator, not a designer describes how generated products start to feel interchangeable, because the models lean toward statistically safe versions of “good UI.” Taste is not a feature starts from the same study to argue that AI makes taste more important, not less. Pretending none of this is happening won’t make it go away.Fewer bad stories, fewer surprising ones. (Illustration by the author, made with the help of AI, based on Doshi & Hauser, Science Advances, 2024)What I can do is be honest about which part of my job was ever really mine. It was never typing out the checkout. It was deciding what a site should feel like, what to leave out, what a client needs even when they ask for something else. The technical know-how is getting cheaper. Taste and a way of seeing aren’t, and that’s the part I intend to sell. I’m not the only designer making that bet: AI is coming for our design jobs, but it can’t touch taste argues that taste, not technical skill, is where a designer’s edge is moving.The part that staysSome say judgment will be automated next, and the machines will end up filling in every cell of the grid. I doubt it. Machines can already predict what moves an audience on average; that’s what recommendation feeds do. What they can’t know is what you want to say, and since creative work is self-expression, that part stays with you.For a lot of people, the only things standing between them and what they wanted to make were money and technique, and those are getting easier to get past. What they make once they’re through is still up to them.I know plenty of people won’t agree with this, including some whose work I really admire. If you’re one of them, I’d like to hear it. Maybe there’s a line I skipped, or one I stepped over too quickly. The comments are open: tell me where you’d draw the line.
